prompt: On a managed cluster where you run the nodes yourself, which of these does the provider take care of?
hint: The provider takes the part that decides.

choices.text: Upgrading the operating system on every worker machine you own
choices.why: In the classic arrangement the node groups are yours to patch and upgrade.

choices.text: Keeping etcd and the API server running and backed up
choices.why: Right. The control plane is the provider's in every managed arrangement.

choices.text: Deciding which pods may talk to which
choices.why: Network policies are yours on every cluster, managed or not (lesson 24).

choices.text: Setting the memory limits your pods run with
choices.why: Limits are in your manifests, and a wrong one fails the same way on any cluster.

prompt: A team moves from a managed cluster with its own node groups to GKE Autopilot. What stops being their job?
hint: Autopilot is the right-hand column of the table.

choices.text: Writing the manifests for their workloads
choices.why: Workloads stay yours in both columns.

choices.text: Granting their colleagues access through RBAC
choices.why: Access stays yours in both columns.

choices.text: Sizing, patching and upgrading the machines the pods run on
choices.why: Right. With Autopilot the provider decides the machines from what the pods request.

choices.text: Paying for the compute that their pods use while they are running
choices.why: They still pay, now for what the pods request rather than for whole machines.

prompt: A pod on a managed cluster keeps running out of memory and restarting. The team opens a ticket with the provider. What should they expect?
hint: Which row of the table holds a memory limit?

choices.text: A fix, since the provider runs the cluster
choices.why: The provider runs the control plane; the pod's limit is in the team's own manifest.

choices.text: A larger node, assigned automatically
choices.why: A bigger node does not raise a container's own limit, which is what it is hitting.

choices.text: To be told it is their workload, which fails the same way anywhere
choices.why: Right. A limit set too low is a workload problem on any cluster, managed or on a laptop.

choices.text: A refund under the uptime commitment
choices.why: The commitment covers the control plane being reachable, which it was.

prompt: According to the pinned AWS price list, how many US dollars per hour does an EKS cluster cost while its version is in standard support?
hint: The first line for each region.

prompt: On GKE, what is the total hourly fee, in US dollars, for a cluster whose version is in extended support?
hint: The extended fee is added to the ordinary one.

prompt: Why is GKE's free tier of 74.40 dollars a month described as one free cluster?
hint: Multiply the hourly fee by the hours in a 31-day month.

choices.text: It equals 0.10 an hour for 744 hours
choices.why: Right: 31 days of 24 hours is 744, and 744 times 0.10 is 74.40.

choices.text: It also pays for the nodes of a small cluster
choices.why: The page says the credits apply to the cluster fee and to no other line, nodes included.

choices.text: Google waives every fee for the first cluster of each project
choices.why: The credit is per billing account, and it covers only the management fee.

choices.text: Regional clusters have no management fee
choices.why: The page says the flat fee applies to every cluster, and the credit only to zonal and Autopilot ones.

prompt: A company's accounts, network and identity are all on Azure. An engineer proposes GKE because its control plane is free on the first cluster. What is the strongest objection?
hint: Where would the cluster's pods need to reach?

choices.text: GKE fails CNCF conformance, so manifests would differ
choices.why: All three are certified; the manifests would be the same.

choices.text: AKS has no free tier at all
choices.why: AKS publishes a free tier too; and the fee is not the deciding cost anyway.

choices.text: The cluster would reach every other system across the internet
choices.why: Right. A fee of a few dozen dollars is small next to wiring a cluster into another cloud's network and identity.

choices.text: GKE's extended support costs more than Azure's
choices.why: This lesson quotes no Azure figure, and support cost is not the main issue here.

prompt: Which of these stay your responsibility on every managed cluster, whichever column of the table you choose? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: The images and manifests of your workloads
choices.why: Right: a broken image fails anywhere.

choices.text: Backing up etcd
choices.why: That is the provider's, with the rest of the control plane.

choices.text: Who may delete a deployment
choices.why: Right: RBAC is written by you.

choices.text: Upgrading the API server
choices.why: The provider upgrades it, when you ask or on its schedule.

choices.text: Which pod may talk to which
choices.why: Right: network policies are yours.

prompt: Match each provider with the name of its arrangement where the provider runs the nodes.
hint: The last row of the table.
